steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our programming languages paper on VL, a surface language and compiler for programming with versions built on the core calculus \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}}. Explain the dependency-update problem, why \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} alone is not practical, what VL and its compiler do, our technical contributions, and the paper outline.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Updating the software packages a project depends on is one of the major issues in software development. A newer version of a package brings improvements, but it also brings the risk of breaking changes, and these can make the whole software defective.

We think this issue comes from a principle that most programming languages follow, namely that only one version of a package can be used at a time. Because of this principle, developers have to decide whether to update to a new, improved version of a package that needs many changes, or to stay with an older version. And the problem gets worse when the package is used indirectly. This dilemma often ends in delays in adopting upgrades, and that leads to stagnation in software development and maintenance.

Programming with versions is a recent proposal where programming languages support multiple versions of programming elements at a time, so the developer can cope flexibly with incompatible changes. The core calculus is \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}}, where a versioned value encapsulates multiple versions of a value (and this includes function values). The type system of \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} checks the consistency of each term, so a value produced in a version is always passed to functions in the same version. The design of the calculus and the type system is based on coeffect calculus.

\lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} gives the essential language constructs for supporting multiple versions in a program, but the language is far from practical. For example, when there are multiple versions of a module, each version of the function has to be represented by hand inside a versioned value (i.e., a record-like expression). \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} is as simple as lambda calculus, but it has a verbose syntax because of the coeffect calculus. So there are aspects of versioning in \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} that a compiler for a surface language could automate.

- VL: surface language for \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} + compilation method
  - imported function name = multi-version term, each occurrence may use a different version
  - VL -> VLMini (version-label-free variant) -> type and version inference -> version-specialized Haskell
  - explicit version control constructs (keep an older version)
- Techniques: (a) Girard's translation VL -> VLMini, (b) bundling, (c) type and version inference; soundness proof; compiler; code generation via z3 (cite)
- Outline: S2 concepts, S3 bundling + Girard, S4 inference, S5 implementation, S6 Haskell library case study, S7 discussion, related work, conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Updating the software packages a project depends on is one of the major issues in software development. A newer version of a package brings improvements, but it also brings the risk of breaking changes, and these can make the whole software defective.

We think this issue comes from a principle that most programming languages follow, namely that only one version of a package can be used at a time. Because of this principle, developers have to decide whether to update to a new, improved version of a package that needs many changes, or to stay with an older version. And the problem gets worse when the package is used indirectly. This dilemma often ends in delays in adopting upgrades, and that leads to stagnation in software development and maintenance.

Programming with versions is a recent proposal where programming languages support multiple versions of programming elements at a time, so the developer can cope flexibly with incompatible changes. The core calculus is \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}}, where a versioned value encapsulates multiple versions of a value (and this includes function values). The type system of \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} checks the consistency of each term, so a value produced in a version is always passed to functions in the same version. The design of the calculus and the type system is based on coeffect calculus.

\lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} gives the essential language constructs for supporting multiple versions in a program, but the language is far from practical. For example, when there are multiple versions of a module, each version of the function has to be represented by hand inside a versioned value (i.e., a record-like expression). \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} is as simple as lambda calculus, but it has a verbose syntax because of the coeffect calculus. So there are aspects of versioning in \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} that a compiler for a surface language could automate.

We propose the functional language VL, which is a surface language for \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}}, together with a compilation method for it. In VL, a function name that is imported from an external module represents a multi-version term, and each occurrence of the function name can refer to a different version of the function. The VL compiler translates a program into an intermediate language called VLMini, which is a variant of \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} without version labels. Then it determines the version of each name occurrence using a type and version inference algorithm, and it translates the program back into a Haskell program that is specialized to versions. VL also has constructs for controlling the versions of expressions explicitly, and these are useful when you want to keep using an older version for some reason.

In this paper we present the following techniques in VL: (a) applying Girard’s translation to translate VL into VLMini, (b) bundling, which makes a top-level function act as a versioned value, and (c) a type and version inference algorithm that identifies the version of each expression with respect to the \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} type system. We also prove that the inference system is sound and we implement a VL compiler. Code generation turns a VL program into a version-specialized Haskell program, using the solution that we get from z3.

Section 2 introduces incompatibility issues and the fundamental concepts of programming with versions, using \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} and VL. Section 3 introduces bundling and Girard’s transformation. Section 4 presents the algorithmic version inference for VL. Section 5 is about the implementation of VL, and Section 6 gives a case study that simulates an incompatible update made in a Haskell library. Section 7 discusses further development of the language, and then the paper ends with related work and a conclusion.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Updating dependent software packages is one of the major issues in software development. Even though a newer version of a package brings improvements, it also carries the risk of breaking changes, which can make the entire software defective.

We argue that this issue originates from the principle, followed by most programming languages, of allowing the use of only one version of a package at a time. Due to this principle, developers must decide either to update to a new, improved version of a package that requires many changes or to remain with an older version. The problem gets worse when a package is used indirectly. This dilemma often results in delays in adopting upgrades, leading to stagnation in software development and maintenance [1,2].

Programming with versions [3,4,5,6] is a recent proposal that allows programming languages to support multiple versions of programming elements at a time, so that developers can flexibly cope with incompatible changes. \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} is the core calculus, in which a versioned value encapsulates multiple versions of a value (including a function value). The \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} type system checks the consistency of each term so that a value produced in a version is always passed to functions in the same version. The design of the calculus and the type system is based on coeffect calculus [7,8].

While \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} offers the essential language constructs for supporting multiple versions in a program, the language is far from practical. For example, with multiple versions of a module, each version of a function must be manually represented inside a versioned value (i.e., a record-like expression). \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} is as simple as lambda calculus, yet its syntax is verbose due to the coeffect calculus. In short, some aspects of versioning in \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} can be automated by a surface language compiler.

We propose the functional language VL as a surface language for \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}}, along with its compilation method. In VL, a function name imported from an external module represents a multi-version term, where each occurrence of the name can reference a different version of the function. The VL compiler translates a program into the intermediate language VLMini, a version-label-free variant of \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}}, determines the version of each name occurrence with a type and version inference algorithm, and translates the result back into a version-specialized Haskell program. VL also offers constructs to explicitly control the versions of expressions, which are useful for continuing to use an older version for some reason.

This paper presents the following techniques in VL: (a) an application of Girard’s translation to translate VL into VLMini, (b) bundling, which makes a top-level function act as a versioned value, and (c) a type and version inference algorithm that identifies the version of each expression with respect to the \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} type system. We also prove the soundness of the inference system and implement a VL compiler, whose code generation converts a VL program into a version-specialized Haskell program using the solution obtained from z3 [9].

Section 2 introduces incompatibility issues and the fundamental concepts of programming with versions with \lambda_{\mathrm{VL}} and VL. Section 3 introduces bundling and Girard’s transformation. Section 4 presents algorithmic version inference for VL. Section 5 describes an implementation of VL, and Section 6 presents a case study simulating an incompatible update made in a Haskell library. Finally, Section 7 discusses further language development, related work, and concludes the paper.
